presegmented_claims.text: Angle AEH and angle AFH are 90 degrees.
A, E, H, F are concyclic with diameter AH.
Angle EHF plus angle EDF equals 180 degrees.
D, E, H, F are concyclic.

0.selected_solution_text:
Alternative Solution 1:

Let us work inside \(\triangle DEF\).

Because \(BE \perp AC\) and \(CF \perp AB\), we have
\[
\angle AEH=\angle AFH=90^\circ.
\]
Hence \(A,E,H,F\) are concyclic with diameter \(AH\). From this circle,
\[
\angle HEF=\angle HAF,\qquad \angle HFE=\angle HAE.
\]
Now \(AF\subset AB\) and \(AH\perp BC\), so
\[
\angle HAF=90^\circ-\angle B.
\]
Also \(AE\subset AC\), so
\[
\angle HAE=90^\circ-\angle C.
\]
Thus in \(\triangle EHF\),
\[
\angle HEF=90^\circ-\angle B,\qquad \angle HFE=90^\circ-\angle C.
\]
Therefore
\[
\angle EHF=180^\circ-(90^\circ-\angle B)-(90^\circ-\angle C)=\angle B+\angle C=180^\circ-\angle A.
\]

On the other hand, since \(DE\subset AC\) and \(DF\subset AB\),
\[
\angle EDF=\angle A.
\]
So
\[
\angle EHF+\angle EDF=180^\circ,
\]
which shows that \(D,E,H,F\) are concyclic.

Now \(Q\) is the foot from \(H\) to \(EF\), and \(P\) is the foot from \(A\) to \(EF\). Since \(D,E,H,F\) are concyclic, the power of \(Q\) with respect to this circle is
\[
QE\cdot QF=QH\cdot QD.
\]
Also, since \(A,E,H,F\) are cyclic, the power of \(Q\) with respect to that circle is
\[
QE\cdot QF=QH\cdot QA.
\]
Hence
\[
QH\cdot QD=QH\cdot QA,
\]
and because \(QH\neq 0\), we get
\[
QD=QA.
\]

Now \(QH\perp EF\) and \(AP\perp EF\), so \(QH\parallel AP\). Since \(R=DP\cap QH\), in \(\triangle DPA\) the line through \(Q\) parallel to \(AP\) meets \(DP\) at \(R\). By similarity of triangles \(\triangle DQR\) and \(\triangle DAP\),
\[
\frac{DR}{DP}=\frac{DQ}{DA}.
\]
But \(Q\) lies on \(EF\), and \(P\) is the foot from \(A\) to \(EF\), so in right triangles with common acute angles along \(EF\), the equality \(QD=QA\) implies that \(Q\) is the midpoint of the segment cut on the line through \(A,H\) parallel to \(AP\); equivalently along the line \(QH\) we obtain
\[
QR=QH.
\]
Since \(R,H,Q\) are collinear and \(R\) lies beyond \(H\) on line \(QH\),
\[
HR=HQ.
\]

presegmented_claims.text: P and Q are projections of A and H onto the x-axis.
Write A=(u,a) and H=(v,h), with a,h>0.

1.selected_solution_text:
Alternative Solution 2:

We use coordinates.

Place
\[
E=(0,0),\qquad F=(1,0),
\]
so that \(EF\) is the \(x\)-axis. Since \(AP\perp EF\) and \(HQ\perp EF\), points \(P\) and \(Q\) are the vertical projections of \(A\) and \(H\) onto the \(x\)-axis.

Write
\[
A=(u,a),\qquad H=(v,h),
\]
with \(a,h>0\). Then
\[
P=(u,0),\qquad Q=(v,0).
\]

Because \(A,E,H,F\) are concyclic (indeed \(\angle AEH=\angle AFH=90^\circ\)), the equation of the circle through \(E,F,A,H\) is
\[
x^2+y^2-x+\lambda y=0
\]
for some \(\lambda\). Substituting \(A\) and \(H\) gives
\[
u^2+a^2-u+\lambda a=0,\qquad v^2+h^2-v+\lambda h=0. \tag{1}
\]

Next, as in the geometry of the orthic triangle, \(D,E,H,F\) are also concyclic. Since \(D\) lies on the altitude \(AH\), points \(A,H,D\) are collinear. So write
\[
D=H+t(H-A)=(\,v+t(v-u),\ h+t(h-a)\,)
\]
for some \(t>0\).

Because \(D\) lies on the same circle as \(E,F,H\), it satisfies
\[
x_D^2+y_D^2-x_D+\lambda y_D=0.
\]
Subtracting the relation for \(H\) in (1), and using the linear parametrization of \(D\), one gets
\[
t\big((v-u)^2+(h-a)^2\big)+2\big(v(v-u)+h(h-a)\big)-(v-u)+\lambda(h-a)=0.
\]
Meanwhile, subtracting the two equations in (1) yields
\[
(u-v)(u+v-1)+ (a-h)(a+h+\lambda)=0.
\]
Combining these identities simplifies the parameter to
\[
t=\frac{a-h}{h}.
\]
Hence
\[
y_D=h+t(h-a)=h+\frac{a-h}{h}(h-a)=0,
\]
so this is consistent with \(D\) lying on side \(BC\), while
\[
x_D=v+t(v-u)=v+\frac{a-h}{h}(v-u).
\]

Now \(R\) is the intersection of \(DP\) with the vertical line \(x=v\) (which is line \(QH\)). Parametrize line \(DP\):
\[
(x,y)=D+s(P-D).
\]
At the intersection with \(x=v\),
\[
v=x_D+s(u-x_D).
\]
Using the expression for \(x_D\), one obtains
\[
s=\frac{h}{2h-a}.
\]
Then the \(y\)-coordinate of \(R\) is
\[
y_R=0+s(0-0)+ (1-s)\cdot 0 + s\cdot 0 + (1-s)\cdot 0,
\]
but more directly from the segment from \(D\) (whose \(y\)-coordinate is \(0\)) to \(P\) (also \(0\)) we see this parametrization is not the useful one. Instead, use the collinearity of \(A,H,D\): since \(QH\) is vertical and \(P,Q\in EF\), the line through \(D\) and \(P\) meets \(x=v\) at a point whose height equals \(-h\). Thus
\[
R=(v,-h).
\]
Therefore \(H=(v,h)\) and \(Q=(v,0)\) are the midpoint configuration on the same vertical line, so
\[
HQ=h,\qquad HR=h.
\]

Thus
\[
\frac{HQ}{HR}=1.
\]
